US-AS.note: American Samoa makes it a felony to carry a firearm concealed on the person, with exemptions only for officers, prison staff and soldiers, and it separately requires an arms license, so there is no permitless carry.

US-GU.note: Guam law forbids carrying a concealed firearm without a license from the Guam Police Department (a shall-issue license under 10 GCA § 60109.1), and it has no permitless-carry law.

US-MP.note: Commonwealth law bars carrying any firearm in public except in listed cases (home, range, hunting, lawful transport in a locked case) and defines a concealed firearm, so there is no permitless concealed carry.

US-VI.note: The V.I. Supreme Court in Heath v. People (2024) upheld convictions under 14 V.I.C. § 2253(a) for possessing firearms without a license, and the VIPD Firearms License Division still requires a license, so there is no permitless carry.

US-MA.note: Automatic restoration upon release from prison.

US-MI.note: Automatic restoration upon release from prison.

US-MN.note: Automatic restoration upon release from prison.

US-MP.note: A person is barred from voting only while serving a sentence for a felony, so the right returns automatically when the sentence ends.

US-MS.note: Specified disqualifying offenses are a permanent bar unless the governor pardons or both houses of the legislature restore the right by a two-thirds vote.

US-MT.note: Automatic restoration upon release from prison.

US-NC.note: Automatic restoration upon completion of sentence (prison, parole and probation).

US-ND.note: Automatic restoration upon release from prison.

US-NH.note: Automatic restoration upon release from prison.

US-NY.note: Automatic restoration upon release from prison.

US-OK.note: Automatic restoration upon completion, discharge or commutation of the original sentence, or a pardon.

US-OR.note: Automatic restoration upon release from prison.

US-PA.note: Automatic restoration upon release from prison. A person convicted of violating Pennsylvania election law is barred for four years after conviction, a narrow election-crime exception.

US-SC.note: Automatic restoration upon completion of sentence (prison, parole and probation).

US-SD.note: Automatic restoration upon completion of sentence (prison, parole and probation).

US-TN.note: People must obtain a court order after completing the sentence and paying restitution and meeting child-support obligations; certain felonies (for example rape, murder, bribery, treason) are permanent bars.

US-TX.note: Automatic restoration upon completion of sentence (prison, parole and probation).

US-UT.note: Automatic restoration upon release from prison.

US-VA.note: On 2026-01-01 the constitution required restoration by the governor case by case; under Department of Elections guidance of September 15, 2026 most people are restored automatically on release from prison, while murder and manslaughter still require an application.

US-AK.note: Alaska's police protection chapter neither creates nor bars a civilian complaint board, so a city or borough may set one up under its own powers.

US-AL.note: Alabama's peace officer standards law says nothing for or against a civilian complaint board, and Birmingham created its own civilian review board by city action in 2021.

US-AR.note: Arkansas's municipal police officers' bill of rights neither creates nor bars a civilian complaint board, so a city may set one up under its own powers.

US-AZ.note: At least two-thirds of any government body that investigates officer misconduct or recommends or imposes discipline must be certified officers from the officer's own department, so a civilian board may only review decisions after the fact.

US-CA.note: Counties may create civilian sheriff oversight boards and an inspector general with subpoena power over the sheriff's department; AB 1185 took effect in 2021 and AB 847 (ch. 383) amended the section effective 1/1/2026.

US-CO.note: Colorado's 2020 police integrity act sets duties for agencies and the state POST board but neither creates nor bars a civilian complaint board, so a city or county may set one up under its own powers, as Denver did.

US-CT.cite: Conn. Gen. Stat. § 7-294aaa (P.A. 20-1, July Special Session)
US-CT.note: A town may by ordinance set up a civilian police review board and may give it power to issue subpoenas and to compel documents; the section refers to boards existing before July 31, 2020, the date the act was signed.

US-DC.note: The District's Office of Police Complaints and Police Complaints Board receive, investigate and adjudicate civilian complaints against Metropolitan Police officers.

US-DE.note: Delaware's police officers' due process chapter neither creates nor bars a civilian board, and a 2022 bill to authorize community oversight boards dropped that provision; Wilmington's complaint board rests on a city ordinance.

US-FL.cite: Fla. Stat. § 112.533(3) (ch. 2024-86, Laws of Fla., HB 601)
US-FL.note: Since 7/1/2024 local governments may not adopt ordinances on investigating police misconduct complaints or on civilian oversight of those investigations; sheriffs and police chiefs may set up civilian boards that only review policies.

US-GA.note: No Georgia statute creates or bars a civilian police board, and the Atlanta Citizen Review Board works under a city ordinance that gives it subpoena power.

US-GU.note: Guam's Community Police Review Commission, first created in 1999 and re-established by Public Law 30-076 on 1/22/2010, receives complaints against Guam Police Department employees, investigates them, holds hearings and may issue subpoenas.

US-HI.note: Chapter 139 created a statewide Law Enforcement Standards Board with a majority of public members (four public and two officers) to certify officers and act on misconduct, though the board was still being staffed in 2026.

US-IA.note: A city with a civil service commission may not adopt or enforce an ordinance or any other measure that creates a board for citizen review of police officers, which ended the boards in Iowa City, Cedar Rapids and other cities.

US-ID.note: Idaho's peace officer standards chapter neither creates nor bars a civilian complaint board, so a city or county may set one up under its own powers.

US-IL.note: Illinois's Uniform Peace Officers' Disciplinary Act neither creates nor bars a civilian complaint board, and Chicago's civilian office and community commission rest on city ordinances.

US-IN.note: Indiana's police merit system chapter neither creates nor bars a civilian complaint board, though a merit board keeps final say over discipline, so a city may set up only an advisory board.

US-KS.note: Kansas's peace officer standards article neither creates nor bars a civilian complaint board, so a city or county may set one up under its own powers.

US-KY.note: No state law requires civilian oversight, and none bars a local board: § 15.520(5) sends a complaint to a law enforcement agency for investigation, and Louisville Metro runs its own civilian review board (Build 3 review, 9/29/2026).

US-LA.note: Louisiana's law enforcement officers' rights chapter sets minimum steps for an investigation but neither creates nor bars a civilian board, and New Orleans' independent police monitor rests on its city charter.

US-MA.note: The Peace Officer Standards and Training Commission, a nine-member board with a civilian majority, has a division of police standards that receives every agency's complaints, investigates officer misconduct and recommends discipline up to decertification.

US-MD.cite: Md. Code, Pub. Safety §§ 3-102, 3-104 (Police Accountability Act of 2021)
US-MD.note: Every county must have a police accountability board that takes public complaints and an administrative charging committee with civilian members that reviews each misconduct investigation, can require more investigation and subpoenas, and decides whether to charge the officer.

US-ME.note: Maine's only statewide complaint body is a committee of the Criminal Justice Academy board that has just two citizen members out of five and investigates certified officers for certification, and no Maine statute creates, requires or bars a local civilian board.

US-MI.note: Michigan's law enforcement standards act neither creates nor bars a civilian complaint board, and Detroit's civilian police commission, with subpoena power, rests on the city charter.

US-MN.note: Local governments may create civilian oversight councils that investigate misconduct after any criminal case, subpoena testimony and documents, and make findings and recommend discipline to the chief.

US-MO.note: Since 2000 cities and counties may create civilian review boards to receive, investigate and make findings on public complaints; a 2024 amendment (SB 754, effective 8/28/2024) limits them to those powers and voids any broader authority.

US-MP.note: The Northern Mariana Islands' public safety department chapter creates no civilian complaint board and nothing in it bars one.

US-MS.note: Mississippi's law enforcement training chapter neither creates nor bars a civilian complaint board, so a city may set one up under its own powers.

US-MT.note: Montana's peace officer standards provisions neither create nor bar a civilian complaint board, so a city or county may set one up under its own powers.

US-NC.note: No state law requires civilian oversight or bars a local board; confidential personnel files and local acts (Charlotte, S.B. 193 of 2021) limit what a board may see and do, and Charlotte, Durham and Raleigh run their own boards (Build 3 review, 9/29/2026).

US-ND.note: North Dakota's peace officer standards chapter neither creates nor bars a civilian complaint board, so a city may set one up under its own powers.

US-NE.note: Nebraska's police standards statutes neither create nor bar a civilian complaint board, so a city may set one up under its own powers.

US-NH.note: The state Conduct Review Committee has four law enforcement members and three public members and reviews misconduct allegations for certification, and no New Hampshire statute creates, requires or bars a local civilian board.

US-NJ.cite: N.J.S.A. 40A:14-118; Fraternal Order of Police, Newark Lodge No. 12 v. City of Newark, 244 N.J. 75 (2020)
US-NJ.note: In 2020 the New Jersey Supreme Court held that a city may not give its civilian review board subpoena power or a role in discipline, because state law leaves those to the police department and the Attorney General's rules, so boards can only advise.

US-NM.note: New Mexico's law enforcement training article neither creates nor bars a civilian complaint board, and Albuquerque's civilian oversight agency rests on a city ordinance.

US-NV.note: Cities and counties may create civilian review boards whose panels review internal investigations, recommend discipline and may subpoena witnesses and documents; they have no jurisdiction over alleged crimes.

US-NY.note: Executive Law section 75 (June 2020) created the Law Enforcement Misconduct Investigative Office, an independent statewide office that receives and investigates complaints of excessive force and other misconduct by officers in more than 500 local agencies.

US-OH.note: Ohio's municipal police chapter neither creates nor bars a civilian complaint board, and Cleveland and Columbus run boards under their own charters.

US-OK.note: No Oklahoma statute creates or bars a civilian police board, and Oklahoma City has one while Tulsa's council took up an oversight ordinance on its own authority.

US-OR.note: Oregon's police records statute names civilian or community oversight boards designated by a city or agency as bodies that investigate allegations of officer misconduct, so state law recognizes local boards and does not limit them.

US-PA.note: No Pennsylvania statute creates or bars civilian police review; Pittsburgh's board, with subpoena power, comes from its home rule charter, though the Commonwealth Court held in 2011 that a state criminal history records law limits which police records it may compel.

US-PR.cite: P.R. Laws Ann. tit. 25, § 3531 et seq. (Ley 20-2017, cap. 2)
US-PR.note: Puerto Rico's police law creates no civilian complaint board and does not bar one, and it placed the police bureau under the Secretary of Public Safety (Law 83-2025 later made it a separate agency).

US-RI.note: The Law Enforcement Officers' Due Process, Accountability, and Transparency Act sets how a law enforcement agency investigates officers and says nothing for or against a civilian board, so Providence's review board rests on its own city law.

US-SC.note: South Carolina's law enforcement training chapter neither creates nor bars a civilian complaint board, so a city may set one up under its own powers.

US-SD.note: South Dakota's law enforcement standards provisions neither create nor bar a civilian complaint board, so a city or county may set one up under its own powers.

US-TN.cite: Tenn. Code Ann. Title 38, Ch. 8 (Pub. Ch. 454, 2023, SB 591)
US-TN.note: The 2023 law abolished community oversight boards and lets cities create police advisory and review committees that send complaints to internal affairs, review its files and may only ask for further investigation; they have no subpoena power.

US-TX.note: Texas law recognizes municipal civilian oversight boards and sets who may serve on one (S.B. 1957, effective 6/20/2025) but neither gives such a board investigative power nor bars a city from creating one.

US-UT.note: A city may not create a board with power independent of the police chief to overrule hiring, veto policy or approve the budget, but the law lets a city appoint an oversight board and does not stop one from reviewing complaints, so state law neither creates nor bars a complaint-review board.

US-VA.note: Localities may create civilian oversight bodies that investigate complaints, issue findings, make binding discipline decisions in serious cases and seek court subpoenas (2020 Special Session I, cc. 29-30).

US-VI.note: The Virgin Islands Police Department chapter creates no civilian complaint board and nothing in it bars one, and the territory has no local governments that could create their own.

US-VT.note: The Vermont Criminal Justice Council takes and adjudicates complaints of officer misconduct for certification but is mostly law enforcement and government members with seven public members, and no Vermont statute creates, requires or bars a local civilian board.

US-WA.note: The 2021 law created the Office of Independent Investigations in the governor's office to investigate police uses of deadly force independently of police agencies; it covers serious incidents, not every complaint.

US-WI.note: State law gives each city's citizen police and fire commission the power to hear charges filed by any aggrieved person against an officer and to impose discipline; it is a hearing board rather than an investigating office.

US-WV.note: West Virginia's law enforcement standards article neither creates nor bars a civilian complaint board, so a city may set one up under its own powers.

US-WY.note: Wyoming's peace officer standards article neither creates nor bars a civilian complaint board, so a city or county may set one up under its own powers.

us-policy-positions:justice-public-safet.note: Yes means state law makes an owner liable, or requires safe storage, when a child can or is likely to get a gun, without waiting for the child to use it.
